The first are more properly called _fenfations_, the last _feelings_. The French word _fentiment_ is common to both?"<x_0.668><y_0.1461><class_Text>

For, for!, The painful fenfations of the animal kind are admonitions to avoid what would hurt us; and the agreeable fenfations of this kind invite us to those actions that are necesitary to the preferation of the individual, or of the kind. Secondly, By the fame means nature invites us to moderate bodily exercise, and admonities us to avoid idlenefs and inactivity on the one hand, and excessive labour and fatigue upon the other. _Thirdly_, The moderate exercise of all our national powers gives pleasure. _Fourthly_, Every species of beauty is behold with pleasure, and every species of deformity with difficult; and we shall find all that we call beautiful, to be something often able, or useful in itself, or a sign of fomething that is estimable or useful. _Fifthly_, The benevolent affections are all accompanied with an agreeable feeling, the malevolent with the contrary. And, _Sixthly_, The high-eff, the nobleft and most durable pleature is that of doing well and acting the part that becomes us; and the most bitter and painful femtiment is the anguish and re-more of a guilty confidence." (See HAPPINESS and PLEASURE). A little reflection may falsify us, that the number and variety of our fenfations and feelings are prodigious. For, to omit all those which accompany our appetites, pattions, and affections, our moral fentiments and fentiments of tafte, even our external fenfes, furniti a great variety of fenfations differing in kind, and almost in every kind an endless variety of degrees. Every variety we discern, with regard to tafte, fmell, found, colour, heat, and cold, and in the tangible qualities of bodies, is indicated by a fenfation correfponding to it.<x_0.6689><y_0.6953><class_Text>

<x_0.0098><y_0.6945>The motif general and the motif important division of our fenfations and feelings is into the agreeable, the differenceable, and the indifferent. Every thing we call pleasure, happiness, or enjoyment, on the one hand; and, on the other, every thing we call mifery, pain, or uneafineft, is fenfation or feeling: For no man can for the prefent be more happy, or more miferable, than he feels himself to be. He cannot be deceived with regard to the enjoyment or suffering of the prefent moment.<x_0.6641><y_0.8156><class_Text>
